paras: The Minneapolis candy store assault was a street confrontation at about 2 a.m. on August 7, 1903, at First Avenue South and Third Street in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in which white men beat a Black man who had been eating ice cream with two white girls. A large crowd then gathered and talked of chasing the city's Black men "to cover" before police broke it up, and a second melee followed. The St. Paul Globe reported it as "something approaching a race riot," and the Minneapolis police were afterward ordered to suppress "demonstrations against colored men."

According to the Globe, Black men and white women walking and dining together had become common in Minneapolis, and Black men had shown a "special tendency" to seek white girls' company since "the Indiana troubles and the lynchings in Southern localities." Police said a feud had arisen over the previous week or two between "a certain class of whites" and Black workers whose jobs kept them downtown all night.

Two Black men were eating ice cream in a candy store with two white girls when two white young men who knew the girls ordered them to leave. When the Black men refused, one was severely beaten and the other escaped. The Globe's follow-up placed the attack on "Thursday night" and said "several white men" took part, while Rev. D. E. Butler described it as "some white men" interfering and a "rough house" following.

A large crowd gathered in the street, with about a dozen Black men nearby, and there was talk of chasing Black residents "to cover" until Patrolman Wold arrived and quelled it. Afterward a white man on the sidewalk who was jostled by a Black man knocked him down, starting a second melee that police again stopped.

No arrests were reported. Prominent Black residents said nothing in the law barred white women from associating with Black men, and Black men threatened to "use weapons in defense of their rights" if assaults continued. Black men married to white women held several meetings to decide how to act if attacked.

Police Superintendent Conroy ordered that anyone of any color creating a street disturbance be arrested, and the department said it would suppress "negro baiting." The next night two unknown white men beat Charles Collins, a Black saloon porter from St. Paul, at Washington and Hennepin; his white wife kept him from using his knife.

The St. Paul Globe, the only paper found to report the episode in either the white or the Black press, covered it in three issues. Its first report, "Race War Brewing in the Mill City," carried the subhead "Foolish White Girls in Company of Black Men Nearly Cause Riotus Outbreak" and quoted white night workers determined to prevent the "plague from spreading." The second, "Police Get Orders to Stop Race War," spoke of "Negro Beating" and quoted a white wife of a Black man who called it "an outrage" that "a few drunken rowdies" should interfere with respectable men "simply because they are black."

On August 10 the paper ran an interview with Butler, superintendent of the St. James social settlement, under the headline "Blacks Indulge Their White Wives." Butler attributed the Minneapolis disturbances to race agitation "all over the country" and said Black residents were doing nothing they had not done for twenty-five or thirty years.

reader.title: Minneapolis candy store assault
bases: White men beat one of two Black men who were with white girls in a candy store, after which a large crowd gathered and talked of chasing Black residents, and a second street melee followed (A1, A2).
All reports come from one paper, the St. Paul Globe (A1, A2), though the paper's interview with Rev. D. E. Butler gives a second, briefer version of the core event (A3).

accounts.label: St. Paul Globe first report
accounts.gist: Two white young men who knew the girls ordered the Black men to leave them; the Black men refused, one was severely beaten and the other escaped, and a crowd gathered until Patrolman Wold arrived.

accounts.label: St. Paul Globe follow-up
accounts.gist: On 'Thursday night' several white men assaulted two Black men seen eating ice cream in a candy store, and a police officer stopped the fight.

accounts.label: Rev. D. E. Butler
accounts.gist: Two Black men ate ice cream with two white women, some white men interfered, and a 'rough house' followed; Butler blamed national race agitation.

framing.detail: The first Globe report, headlined 'Race War Brewing in the Mill City' with the subhead 'Foolish White Girls in Company of Black Men Nearly Cause Riotus Outbreak', blamed interracial association and Black men's 'tendency to seek the society of white girls' rather than the assailants.
The follow-up, 'Police Get Orders to Stop Race War', called it 'Negro Beating' and gave space to a white wife who called the assailants 'drunken rowdies'.
The Butler interview ran under 'Blacks Indulge Their White Wives', leading with his remarks on intermarriage before his account of the disturbances.

conflicts.note: Probably the same night: 2 a.m. Friday, August 7 falls within what the follow-up loosely called Thursday night.

versions.value: Two white young men acquainted with the girls

conflicts.note: The first and fullest report gives two; later, briefer accounts give a vaguer larger number.
